title: Trump-Backed Ken Paxton Crushed John Cornyn by 27 Points in Texas. The November Race Could Decide the Senate.
excerpt: The scandal-plagued attorney general rode a last-minute Trump endorsement to a landslide runoff victory. He will face 37-year-old Democrat James Talarico in a state with 700,000 Indian Americans.
body:
Texas Attorney General Ken Paxton demolished four-term U.S. Senator John Cornyn in Tuesday's Republican Senate runoff, winning by roughly 27 percentage points after securing President Donald Trump's endorsement just one week ago. The Associated Press called the race shortly after polls closed, and what followed at Paxton's election night party in Plano — chants of "Ken, Ken, Ken" echoing through a Dallas suburb — was a definitive display of the MAGA movement's grip on Republican politics.

## The Margin Was Not Close

With 63 percent of the vote counted, Paxton was leading 62.7 percent to Cornyn's 37.3 percent. This was not a competitive runoff. It was a demolition. Cornyn, 74, who served as Senate Republican Whip and had the backing of virtually every establishment Republican in Washington, was outrun by a 63-year-old attorney general who has been indicted on felony securities fraud charges, impeached by his own party's state legislature, and acquitted in a Senate trial that split Texas Republicans down the middle.

None of it mattered. Trump endorsed, and Trump's voters delivered.

## Why This Matters Beyond Texas

Paxton will face Democratic state Representative James Talarico, a 37-year-old Presbyterian seminarian and prolific fundraiser, in a November general election that could determine control of the United States Senate. Talarico has built his campaign on appealing to independents and moderate voters — exactly the voters that Paxton's nomination was designed to repel.

Senate Republicans' own campaign arm warned in an internal memo that a Paxton nomination "would hand Democrats an opening to flip Texas and cause Republicans to divert hundreds of millions of dollars that would otherwise be spent winning key battlegrounds." Senator Lisa Murkowski of Alaska said she was "supremely disappointed" by Trump's endorsement, adding bluntly: "I think that this puts that seat in jeopardy."

If Democrats flip Texas — a state that has not elected a Democratic senator since 1988 — the Senate math changes dramatically. And the race is expected to become one of the most expensive in U.S. history.

## The Diaspora Angle

Texas is home to more than 700,000 Indian Americans, concentrated in Houston, Dallas-Fort Worth, Austin, and San Antonio. The state's Senate race is not an abstraction for this community. Paxton, as attorney general, has been one of the most aggressive enforcers of the Trump administration's immigration policies, filing lawsuits to block DACA protections and challenging visa programs that directly affect H-1B workers and their families.

Talarico, meanwhile, has positioned himself as a voice for working families and has explicitly courted the state's growing South Asian electorate. For Indian Americans in Texas — many of them in the technology and medical sectors that powered the state's economic boom — the choice in November will be unusually stark.

## What Cornyn Said

Cornyn conceded gracefully. "I've said throughout this race that I trust the voters of Texas, and they made their decision, and I must respect it," he said in his concession speech. He pledged to back the Republican ticket in November.

Paxton, for his part, sounded like a man already running a general election campaign. "Without a shadow of a doubt, I will be the Democrats' No. 1 target in November," he said. "Texas will be the radical left's No. 1 priority, but we're not going to let them take it."

## The Bigger Picture

The Texas result is the clearest evidence yet that Trump's endorsement remains the single most powerful force in Republican primary politics. Cornyn had the money, the institutional support, the seniority, and the track record. Paxton had Trump. It was not a fair fight.

For the Indian American community in Texas and beyond, the November race offers a direct referendum on the direction of immigration policy, visa reform, and the broader question of whether the Republican Party's rightward shift has created an opening for Democrats in the nation's second-largest state.
author: Diaspora Desk
